analysis.one_liner: Bans insured banks and credit unions from making or financing payday loans.
analysis.headline: The bill to prohibit payday loans made through banks never left the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal lending law to bar any creditor from making a payday loan when the borrower's check or account is held at an insured bank or credit union, and would prohibit insured banks themselves from making payday loans directly or indirectly — including lending money to payday lenders to finance their loans. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who take short-term payday loans against their bank accounts would be protected from a product widely criticized for trapping people in repeat borrowing at high fees. Bank customers generally would also benefit from having insured institutions out of the payday business.

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit any creditor from making a payday loan secured by a check or account at an insured bank or credit union, cutting off the channel that payday lenders use to collect directly from borrowers' bank accounts.
It would bar insured depository institutions from making payday loans themselves, directly or indirectly, or from lending money to other lenders to finance, refinance, or extend payday loans.

The bill defines a payday loan as a short-term cash advance in exchange for a deferred personal check or an authorization to debit the borrower's account for the advance plus a fee, covering both common structures of the product.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders would lose the legal structure of their product and any bank financing behind it. Some borrowers who rely on payday loans for short-term cash would have to find alternatives, including bank overdrafts or other credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders and their bank financiers

drawbacks.text: Payday loans are used by households that cannot get credit elsewhere, and an outright prohibition would leave some of them with no source of emergency cash, forcing reliance on options like bank overdraft fees or unregulated lenders.
The bill addresses only loans tied to insured banks and credit unions; lenders and borrowers using accounts outside the insured system would fall outside the prohibition's reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is removing a product that can be renewed repeatedly with fees that far exceed the original loan, and it closes off bank financing of that product. The real cost is for borrowers who depend on payday loans as their only source of quick cash; a prohibition protects them only if other credit is available, and the bill offered no replacement option. It also had a structural gap, since it keyed the ban to checks and accounts at insured institutions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Akaka introduced the bill on October 17, 2005, with introductory remarks, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The Senate Banking Committee never reported the bill, and no floor vote was ever held in the Senate.
The bill had one Democratic cosponsor.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and all bills not enacted expire with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders kept operating as before, with their bank-account collection channel and any bank financing intact; the committee never had to take a position on the product.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders, who kept operating unchanged

for.name: Sen. Daniel Akaka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on October 17, 2005.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

against.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee under his chairship never scheduled action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of support and opposition on the merits never appeared in the record; the bill's two supporters were both Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have cut off their core mechanism — collecting repayment through a borrower's check or bank account — and any bank financing behind it. Their business depends on fees charged on short-term advances, often repeatedly rolled over.
The bill would bar them from making payday loans directly or indirectly and from lending to payday lenders to finance, refinance, or extend such loans, eliminating any revenue from that activity.
